other_side: Zitron argues the AI boom depends on perpetual, accelerating revenue, continued debt access and continued venture funding, and describes the finances as "hundreds of billions invested to make single-digit billions". He cites Anthropic's reported 16.8 billion dollars of third-quarter revenue against over 413 billion dollars of non-cancellable compute contracts, and says roughly 80 per cent of the top labs' enterprise revenue comes from loss-making startups. He wrote before the full filing appeared.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether growth can outrun the compute bill. Both accept as fact that Anthropic reported 16.3 billion dollars of first-half revenue, that non-cancellable compute commitments are above 400 billion dollars, and that the company itself says growth will slow by an unknown amount. The empirical question is whether revenue quality is as strong as the filing suggests; the observable is the first audited quarters after the listing, especially customer concentration, margins and net revenue retention. The filing shows 11,900 customers spending over 100,000 dollars a year and a first operating profit, which answers part of Zitron's worry about start-up resellers, but the listing has not yet tested his claim that spending is subsidised. The residue is worldview about whether enterprise demand will broaden. For Whittemore to be vindicated, growth must keep outrunning the bill for several quarters. For Zitron, growth must stall or margins fall once subsidies end. Both are polemicists with incentives, Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron certain of a bubble and anti-hype. The signal is that both treat commitments as the fixed cost that matters. Watch the first post-listing quarterly report.
